title: 62% of Bangladeshi children lack basic maths skills, MICS shows
excerpt: 61.51% of children aged 7 to 14 cannot do the four basic maths operations, MICS 2025 shows, and few secondary maths teachers hold maths degrees.

image.alt: Rows of empty wooden desks and chairs in a classroom in Bangladesh
image.credit: File photo: Tuhin / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: Almost two in three children aged 7 to 14 in Bangladesh cannot do basic addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, according to the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, Bonik Barta reported on Saturday (28 November).

The survey's District Atlas, published by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF on 24 November, found that 61.51% of children in this age group could not perform the four basic operations, the newspaper said. Children of this age are usually in classes two to nine. Under the curriculum, pupils should master all four operations by class three.

In no division could half of children do the four operations. The share who could was lowest in Mymensingh, at 33.91%, followed by Barishal (34.94%), Sylhet (36.25%) and Rangpur (39.17%). Chattogram stood at 39.69% and Dhaka at 39.81%. Only Khulna (43.27%) and Rajshahi (40.91%) were above 40%.

Bonik Barta also cited Bangladesh Education Statistics 2025, which shows that of 67,697 teachers teaching maths at secondary level, only 9,918 (14.65%) hold a bachelor's or master's degree in maths. Another 38,231 (56.47%) have not studied maths beyond higher secondary level. In this year's SSC exam 37.75% of candidates failed, and about a quarter of all candidates failed maths, according to education board data cited by the paper.

Professor Mohammad Nure Alam Siddique of Dhaka University's Institute of Education and Research told Bonik Barta that rote learning was a main cause: teachers still have pupils memorise times tables without explaining why the answers are right. Professor Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel, director general of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, said about 88,000 teacher posts were vacant in government and private schools, and recruitment of 700 teachers for government schools was nearly complete. Primary and Mass Education State Minister Bobby Hajjaj said the government was focusing on pre-primary education in remote areas, trained teachers and play-based learning, and that a new monitoring system looks at what children actually learn.

Why it matters

Enrolment in Bangladesh is high, but these figures show many children move up through school without the foundations they need for later classes, jobs and daily life. The gaps are widest in Mymensingh, Barishal and Sylhet. The same atlas also maps wide district gaps in child marriage and fertility. NGOs running remedial classes, learning centres and teacher training can use the district data to target support. The World Bank’s $300 million primary education financing includes a basic literacy and numeracy package, and these figures give a baseline to measure it against.

What to watch

  • District-level numeracy and reading figures in the full MICS 2025 atlas.
  • Progress on filling about 88,000 vacant teacher posts through PSC and NTRCA.
  • Whether the new primary monitoring system publishes learning-outcome data.

Sources

  • Bonik Barta: 60% of class three to nine students cannot solve even basic maths problems (Bangla), 28 November 2026
  • UNICEF Bangladesh: Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025
